groupings.title: Hoichi the Earless
groupings.summary: On the quiet shores of Dan-no-ura, a blind musician is summoned to play for a mysterious audience.

posts.title: Hoichi the Earless
posts.summary: A blind musician is summoned to perform before a noble court. But the court is not of the living.

blocks.text: The Haunted Shore

Many years ago, in the narrow straits at Dan-no-ura, two great clans met in a final, terrible battle. The Heike and the Genji. The Heike were destroyed, warriors and nobles pulled beneath the waves. And as their cries fell silent, the emperor's grandmother chose to drown her previous grandson, rather than let him be captured and humiliated by his enemy.
The sea remembers that day.

Fishermen still speak of strange lights drifting over the water at night—pale, flickering flames they call oni-bi. When storms roll in, the wind carries a sound like distant battle. And sometimes, in the quiet between waves, there are voices.
A temple was built to soothe the restless dead: Amidaji. Nearby, a cemetery marked the resting place of the fallen.
Prayers were offered daily.
But still, the dead were never entirely at peace.

In this place lived Hoichi. Blind from childhood, he was trained in the biwa and the recitation of history. His voice was clear, precise, expressive. When he sang of Dan-no-ura, listeners wept. It was said even the spirits could not resist his telling.

Hoichi had very little at first. But the priest of Amidaji took pity on him, providing a room, food, and shelter. In return, Hoichi played on quiet evenings, his flawless music and his perfect voice carrying over the narrow straits.
It was a simple life.
And a peaceful one.
Until the night when someone came for him.
The Summons
It was a hot night in summer, the air smelling of brine and kelp, and the cicadas sounding among the pines above the temple.
The priest had been called away. Unable to sleep in the heavy air, Hoichi sat on the veranda, biwa across his lap, the garden beyond him perfectly still.
He heard footsteps approaching.
They were not hesitant. They were heavy and deliberate.
They stopped directly in front of him.
"Hoichi."
The voice was deep and commanding.
"I am blind," Hoichi replied. "I cannot see who calls."
"There is nothing to fear. My lord, a man of high rank, is staying nearby. He has heard of your gifts, Hoichi. You will come with me and perform."
Hoichi could tell that it was not a request. He was being summoned, and he dared not refuse.
Hoichi rose, took his instrument, and followed.
Metal shifted with each step of the summoner who walked in front of him. He was a warrior.
They moved quickly. Faster than Hoichi thought possible. Soon they passed through a great gate, which opened without a word.
Hoichi listened with great care as they walked. The sounds of a garden. Then onward, into the sounds of an echoing hallway, their quick steps along polished floors.
He heard voices. They were soft and refined, and to his ears, unmistakably noble, the sing-song words of Heian-kyō, the words of old poems and courtly tales from the Imperial Capital.
Hoichi heard the voices grow louder as he was guided into a large hall. He was made to sit upon a cushion, elevated on what he was certain to be stage.
A woman spoke, her voice dignified and eternal:
"You will recite for us the story of the Battle of Dan-no-ura."
He began.

The biwa came alive beneath his hands — oars cutting water, arrows splitting air, ships colliding, steel ringing against steel. His voice carried the rise and fall of battle, the chaos, the grief of inevitable defeat.
The room held its breath.

At last, Hoichi reached the final scene. The last moments of the Emperor Antoku, at only six years old. The battle lost, the house of Heike defeated. And so, the once-mighty Kiyomori's widow carries her beloved grandson into the dark waters, telling him of a palace beneath the waves, choosing death over surrender to the Genji.
There was a silence at first from his audience. Then they fell into grief, an open, unguarded, and inconsolable weeping. The men as well as the women, and even the small wailing of a young child.
Hoichi faltered. He had moved audiences before. He had never shaken a room like this.
At last, the woman spoke again.
"You will return tomorrow night. You will recite the story again."
A pause.
"Tell no one."
He was led back before dawn.
He said nothing.

sections.title: Part 3 — The Truth in the Dark

blocks.text: The Truth in the Dark
The summons came again.
And again.
Each night Hoichi left. And each morning he returned quieter, his body worn at the edges in a way that sleep did not repair.
The priest noticed the change. He could see his friend suffering.
But his questions received only careful, vague answers.
So the priest told two of his servants to follow him.
That night, they did, but lost him almost immediately. The sightless Hoichi moved through the dark faster than he should have been able.
The servants searched.
They found nothing. They turned back to tell their master.
But then, near the shore, they heard it: the sound of the biwa.
And they could hear the story of Dan-no-ura.
They followed the sounds to the cemetery.
Light from their lanterns fell over the headstones, and they stopped.
Between the grave markers were of pale flames drifting above the ground, hovering without wind, without source. Countless lights.
And in their center, seated before the tomb of the drowned emperor, was Hoichi.
The rain was falling around him. His voice was raised in full performance. His face turned toward nothing.
The dead were listening.
The servants seized his shoulders, shouted his name. He fought them.
"You must not interrupt," Hoichi said. "This is an august gathering!"
The servants dragged him away.
Once back at the temple, before the priest, Hoichi recounted what had been happening to him.
The priest listened without speaking, focusing on every detail of Hoichi's account.
Then:
"You have not been visiting a lord's court," the priest said.
Hoichi heard the priest pause, and almost hesitate.
"Hoichi... you have been performing for the dead of Dan-no-ura."
The Price
The priest knew that the ghosts would continue this forever, that they would never let Hoichi stop.
There was only one way to protect him.
Before nightfall, the priest and an assistant covered Hoichi's body in sacred text — sutras written in careful strokes across every surface. Chest, back, face, hands, feet, the backs of his fingers.
"These will hide you", the priest said. "Do not speak. Do not move. No matter what you hear."
The night came and Hoichi waited.
He was still and silent, as the priest had instructed.
He heard the heavy footsteps.
The gate.
The garden.
And now, his summoner, directly in front of him.
"Hoichi."
He did not answer.
"Hoichi."
He was silent.
A third time — sharper, irritated.
Hoichi kept himself still.
The figure moved closer. Hoichi heard the shift of armored weight, the soft displacement of air. Felt the presence of something immense and very old leaning over him.
When the voice came again, it was almost to itself:
"I see the instrument…"
A pause.
"…but the player—"
Hoichi could feel something changed in the air.
"There is nothing here."
The pause that followed had the quality of a held breath.
"Nothing..."
Hoichi dared not take a breath.
"Aside from the ears."
Hoichi held firm as the summoner seized them.
It was hard. Violent. Final.
And then they were gone.
Hoichi did not cry out.
He did not move.
And the summoner left.
At dawn, the priest found him where he had been left — seated on the veranda, the floor beneath him dark and wet.
The priest was his simple mistake.
The sutras had covered his body.
But not his ears.
But Hoichi had survived, and his wounds healed.
People came from distant places to hear him — not just for the skill that had always been extraordinary, but for what that skill had cost.
Hoichi was famous. He continued to recite The Tale of the Heike, and brought his listeners to tears when he recounted the Battle of Dan-no-ura, and told of the palace beneath the waves.
And by that time, he was known by a new name:
Hoichi the Earless.
